title: microsoft/PyRIT — Open-source AI red teaming toolkit from Microsoft. Test generative AI systems with automated scans, adaptive multi-turn attacks, and a web UI.
content:
PyRIT (Python Risk Identification Tool for generative AI) is an open-source toolkit for finding security and safety weaknesses in generative AI systems through automated scans, adaptive multi-turn attacks, and human-led testing.
Built by the Microsoft AI Red Team and an open-source community of contributors, PyRIT brings a command-line scanner, a graphical interface, and an extensible Python framework together in one toolkit.
You do not need to be a Microsoft employee or an experienced red teamer to get involved. Join our Discord community to ask questions, exchange techniques, share what you are building, and connect with maintainers and other users.
Contributions include code, documentation, examples, bug reports, testing, and feedback from real-world use. Read the contributor guide and explore issues labeled "help wanted".
Get started | Join Discord | Read the whitepaper
- Scanner: Run repeatable assessments from the command line.
- CoPyRIT GUI: Explore AI systems interactively and review results in your browser.
- Python framework: Compose and extend components to build custom red teaming workflows.
Visit our website for installation, configuration, demos, and documentation. Use the version picker to match the docs to your installation; the guides above follow the latest development version.
Connect to OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Microsoft Foundry, Azure Machine Learning, Google Gemini, Google Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock, Hugging Face, Ollama, Groq, OpenRouter, Cohere, and GitHub Copilot.
Use OpenAI-compatible APIs or built-in targets, or install the optional LiteLLM adapter for additional provider integrations. See the provider configuration guide and LiteLLM provider directory for setup and more providers. Available features depend on the target and model.
Test complete applications and other endpoints through HTTP, WebSockets, browser automation with Playwright, or custom targets.
Read PyRIT: Democratizing AI Red Teaming Through Open-Source Tooling
for the design principles and real-world experience behind the toolkit.
If you use PyRIT in your research, please cite the paper using
CITATION.cff.
To report vulnerabilities in PyRIT privately through the Microsoft Security Response Center, follow our security policy.
This project may contain trademarks or logos for projects, products, or services. Authorized use of Microsoft trademarks or logos is subject to and must follow Microsoft's Trademark & Brand Guidelines. Use of Microsoft trademarks or logos in modified versions of this project must not cause confusion or imply Microsoft sponsorship. Any use of third-party trademarks or logos are subject to those third-party's policies.

report.summary: Microsoft's open-source PyRIT toolkit helps teams red-team generative AI with automated scans, adaptive multi-turn attacks, a GUI, and extensible Python workflows.
report.background: Generative AI systems introduce security and safety risks that traditional software testing does not fully cover, including prompt injection, jailbreaks, harmful outputs, data leakage, and unsafe tool use. Red teaming, long used in cybersecurity, has become a key practice for probing these weaknesses before and after deployment. Microsoft's AI Red Team built PyRIT to make its internal methods more repeatable and accessible, then open-sourced the toolkit with community contributions. The project reflects a broader industry shift: AI vendors, enterprises, and researchers increasingly need shared tooling to test models and full applications across many providers. PyRIT's support for major model APIs, local models, and application endpoints lowers the barrier to structured AI risk assessment.
key_points: PyRIT combines three ways to work: a command-line scanner for repeatable assessments, the CoPyRIT browser GUI for interactive exploration, and a Python framework for composing custom red-teaming workflows. This lets beginners start quickly while giving experienced testers room to extend components and automate deeper checks.

The toolkit connects to many AI providers and targets, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Hugging Face, Ollama, Groq, and GitHub Copilot. It supports OpenAI-compatible APIs, built-in targets, and an optional LiteLLM adapter, so teams can test across models without rebuilding their workflow.

PyRIT focuses on adaptive multi-turn attacks and automated scans, not just single prompts. It can test complete applications through HTTP, WebSockets, browser automation with Playwright, or custom targets. That matters because real AI risks often emerge across conversations and integrated system behavior.

The project is explicitly community-oriented. Microsoft says users do not need to be employees or experienced red teamers to participate; contributors can join Discord, read the contributor guide, explore help-wanted issues, and share code, documentation, examples, bug reports, and real-world feedback.

PyRIT is backed by a whitepaper and citation guidance, signaling that it is intended for both practical security work and research. Its open-source license and extensible design make it a candidate for standardizing AI red-team methods across organizations and toolchains.
report.impact: PyRIT lowers the barrier to professional AI red teaming. For the AI industry, it pushes safety and security testing toward shared, repeatable methods rather than ad hoc internal exercises, and it pressures model providers to make their systems testable across APIs and applications. For developers, it offers a practical way to probe chatbots, agents, and integrated AI features for prompt injection, jailbreaks, and unsafe behavior, and to build custom assessments into their workflows. For regular users, the indirect benefit is safer, more robust AI products as testing becomes more common. The dual-use nature of attack tooling means governance, responsible disclosure, and clear usage policies remain important.
report.tools: Start with PyRIT's scanner, CoPyRIT GUI, and Python framework. The optional LiteLLM adapter broadens provider coverage, while Playwright supports browser-based application testing. For comparison, watch open-source LLM security scanners such as NVIDIA Garak and evaluation-focused tools like Promptfoo. Teams can combine PyRIT with their existing CI, logging, and vulnerability-management systems to turn red-team findings into repeatable checks.
